# Merge Two Sorted Lists — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/linked-list/merge-two-sorted.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Linked List** · easy · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-two-sorted-lists/)

Given the heads of two sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted list by splicing existing nodes (no new value nodes) and return its head.

## What the input promises

- 0 <= each list length <= 50
- -100 <= node value <= 100
- both lists are sorted ascending
- either list may be empty

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `a = 1 → 3 → 5, b = 2 → 4` | `1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5` | — |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. Repeatedly take the smaller of the two front nodes.
2. A dummy head node kills every "is this the first node?" special case.
3. When one list runs out, the other is already sorted — attach the whole remainder.

</details>

---

## 1. Collect and sort

Dump both lists into one array, sort, rebuild. Throws away the pre-sorted structure — O(n log n) where merging is linear.

```python
def merge_sorted(a, b):
    vals = []
    for head in (a, b):
        while head:
            vals.append(head.val)
            head = head.next
    head = None
    for v in sorted(vals, reverse=True):
        head = Node(v, head)
    return head
```

**O((n+m) log (n+m)) time · O(n+m) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public Node mergeSorted(Node a, Node b){
    List<Integer> vals = new ArrayList<>();
    for (Node head : new Node[]{a,b}){
        while (head != null){
            vals.add(head.val);
            head = head.next;
        }
    }
    Collections.sort(vals, Comparator.reverseOrder());
    Node head = null;
    for (int v : vals){
        head = new Node(v, head);
    }
    return head;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
Node* mergeSorted(const Node* a, const Node* b){
    vector<int> vals;
    for (const Node* head : {a,b}){
        while (head){
            vals.push_back(head->val);
            head = head->next;
        }
    }
    sort(vals.rbegin(), vals.rend());
    Node* head = nullptr;
    for (int v : vals){
        head = new Node(v, head);
    }
    return head;
}
```

</details>

## 2. Recursive

> **Why now.** Sorting the combined values throws away the fact that both inputs are already sorted. Merging compares the two heads and never looks back.

The smaller head owns the merge of everything else. Reads beautifully; n+m stack frames make it a demo, not a default.

```python
def merge_sorted(a, b):
    if not a or not b:
        return a or b
    if a.val <= b.val:
        a.next = merge_sorted(a.next, b)
        return a
    b.next = merge_sorted(a, b.next)
    return b
```

**O(n+m) time · O(n+m) stack space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public ListNode mergeSorted(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
    if (a == null || b == null) return a != null ? a : b;
    if (a.val <= b.val) { a.next = mergeSorted(a.next, b); return a; }
    else { b.next = mergeSorted(a, b.next); return b; }
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
ListNode* mergeSorted(ListNode* a, ListNode* b) {
    if (!a || !b) return a ? a : b;
    if (a->val <= b->val) { a->next = mergeSorted(a->next, b); return a; }
    else { b->next = mergeSorted(a, b->next); return b; }
}
```

</details>

---

## 3. The one to remember

> **Why now.** The recursion is that same merge with a stack frame per node. A dummy head and a tail pointer do it in a loop, in constant space.

Create a dummy node and a tail pointer at it. While both lists are non-empty, attach the smaller head to tail and advance that list. When one empties, attach the survivor's remainder in one assignment. Return dummy.next. The dummy means the first comparison needs no special handling.

```python
def merge_sorted(a, b):
    dummy = tail = Node(0)
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else:
            tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b
    return dummy.next
```

**O(n + m) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public ListNode mergeSorted(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);
    ListNode tail = dummy;
    while (a != null && b != null) {
        if (a.val <= b.val) { tail.next = a; a = a.next; }
        else { tail.next = b; b = b.next; }
        tail = tail.next;
    }
    tail.next = (a != null) ? a : b;
    return dummy.next;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
ListNode* mergeSorted(ListNode* a, ListNode* b) {
    ListNode* dummy = new ListNode(0);
    ListNode* tail = dummy;
    while (a && b) {
        if (a->val <= b->val) { tail->next = a; a = a->next; }
        else { tail->next = b; b = b->next; }
        tail = tail->next;
    }
    tail->next = a ? a : b;
    return dummy->next;
}
```

</details>

---

## The arc

One fact carries all three rungs: at any moment the smallest node left anywhere is one of the two heads, so the whole merge is a sequence of single comparisons and no node is ever looked at twice. Dumping both lists into an array and sorting throws that fact away and pays n log n to rediscover an order that arrived for free. Recursion keeps the fact — the smaller head owns the merge of everything behind it — and reads beautifully at a stack frame per node. The loop keeps the fact and drops the frames: a dummy node to hang the result from, a tail pointer to append to, and one assignment at the end to splice on whichever list still has nodes, because that remainder is already sorted. The dummy is the piece to know cold. It removes the question of whether this is the first node from this problem, from merge-k-lists, from remove-list-elements, and from every builder that would otherwise special-case its own head.

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Collect and sort | O((n+m) log (n+m)) time · O(n+m) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | Recursive | O(n+m) time · O(n+m) stack space | Sorting the combined values throws away the fact that both inputs are already sorted. Merging compares the two heads and never looks back. |
| 3 | The one to remember | O(n + m) time · O(1) space | The recursion is that same merge with a stack frame per node. A dummy head and a tail pointer do it in a loop, in constant space. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
# A block is free to declare its own node class and most do; the three that
# CONSTRUCT one without declaring it (reverse-list's array rung, two merge
# rungs) would raise NameError with no scaffolding at all. Declared only when
# absent, so a block's own class always wins.
try: Node
except NameError:
    class Node:
        def __init__(self, val=0, next=None): self.val, self.next = val, next
try: ListNode
except NameError:
    class ListNode:
        def __init__(self, val=0, next=None): self.val, self.next = val, next
try: TreeNode
except NameError:
    class TreeNode:
        def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
            self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

# What the driver BUILDS with is private, because Python is duck-typed: every
# block walks .val/.next or .val/.left/.right and none of them checks a type.
class __LN:
    def __init__(self, v): self.val, self.next = v, None

class __TN:
    def __init__(self, v): self.val, self.left, self.right = v, None, None

def __mklist(vals, cyc=-1):
    if not vals: return None
    ns = [__LN(v) for v in vals]
    for a, b in zip(ns, ns[1:]): a.next = b
    if cyc >= 0: ns[-1].next = ns[cyc]
    return ns[0]

def __mktree(vals):
    if not vals or vals[0] is None: return None
    root = __TN(vals[0]); q = [root]; i = 0; k = 1
    while i < len(q) and k < len(vals):
        node = q[i]; i += 1
        if k < len(vals):
            x = vals[k]; k += 1
            if x is not None: node.left = __TN(x); q.append(node.left)
        if k < len(vals):
            x = vals[k]; k += 1
            if x is not None: node.right = __TN(x); q.append(node.right)
    return root

def merge_sorted_collect_and_sort(a, b):
    vals = []
    for head in (a, b):
        while head:
            vals.append(head.val)
            head = head.next
    head = None
    for v in sorted(vals, reverse=True):
        head = Node(v, head)
    return head


def merge_sorted_recursive(a, b):
    if not a or not b:
        return a or b
    if a.val <= b.val:
        a.next = merge_sorted_recursive(a.next, b)
        return a
    b.next = merge_sorted_recursive(a, b.next)
    return b


def merge_sorted_the_one_to_remember(a, b):
    dummy = tail = Node(0)
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else:
            tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b
    return dummy.next

def __canon_list(h):
    out = []
    while h is not None:
        if len(out) > 10000: return "!CYCLE"
        out.append(str(h.val)); h = h.next
    return "[" + ",".join(out) + "]"

def __canon_tree(t):
    out = []; q = [t]; i = 0
    while i < len(q) and len(q) < 4096:
        n = q[i]; i += 1
        if n is None:
            out.append("null"); continue
        out.append(str(n.val)); q.append(n.left); q.append(n.right)
    while out and out[-1] == "null": out.pop()
    return "[" + ",".join(out) + "]"

def __canon(v):
    if isinstance(v, bool): return "true" if v else "false"
    if isinstance(v, str): return v
    if v is None: return "null"
    if isinstance(v, (list, tuple)):
        return "[" + ",".join(__canon(x) for x in v) + "]"
    # a tree first: a TreeNode has no .next, but a node with .left is never a list
    if hasattr(v, "left") or hasattr(v, "right"): return __canon_tree(v)
    if hasattr(v, "next"): return __canon_list(v)
    return str(v)

APPROACHES = [
    merge_sorted_collect_and_sort,
    merge_sorted_recursive,
    merge_sorted_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# the tail left over when one list runs out first — [5] against [1,2,3] drains b entirely before a moves, and two empties have no dummy to return
CASES = [
    lambda: (__mklist([1,2,4], -1), __mklist([1,3,4], -1)),
    lambda: (__mklist([], -1), __mklist([], -1)),
    lambda: (__mklist([], -1), __mklist([0], -1)),
    lambda: (__mklist([5], -1), __mklist([1,2,3], -1)),
    lambda: (__mklist([1,1], -1), __mklist([1,1], -1)),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(__canon(fn(*make())))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<34} -> {answers}")
```
